Grinding department managers repeatedly complained that their overhead allocation seemed too low compared to Kilning, where maintenance activity was clearly more intensive.
4-13.question: Was the direct method masking the real cost profile?
4-13.insight: A switch to the reciprocal method (implemented in Excel with the Solver add-in) revealed that direct method had UNDER-allocated $180k of maintenance cost to Kilning and OVER-allocated $95k to Grinding. Kilning's true product cost was $2.30/tonne higher than reported; Grinding's was $1.10/tonne lower. Pricing on Grinding's specialty grades was raised 4% with no customer loss — annualized margin gain: $520k.

4-14.v: ⚠️ Scope note — standard cost variances are examined under CMA Part 1 Section C (Performance Management), not Section D. The full treatment lives in Section 3, units 3-1 to 3-5, together with the practice questions. This unit is kept as a quick reference; it is excluded from mock exams and readiness scoring.
What Are Standard Costs?
Predetermined benchmark costs for materials, labor, and overhead — used as a control tool to measure actual performance and compute variances.

Standard costs are PREDETERMINED BENCHMARKS for what costs SHOULD BE under efficient operating conditions. When actual costs differ from standard costs, the difference is a VARIANCE. Variance analysis tells management WHERE costs got out of control and WHY.
Standard Costs & the Flexible Budget

A budget adjusted (flexed) to the ACTUAL level of activity achieved, using standard prices and rates. It answers: 'what SHOULD costs have been for the output we actually produced?' Variances compare actual results to this flexible budget — not to the original static (master) budget.

Standard costs feed the flexible budget: flexible-budget cost = standard cost per unit × actual units produced. The gap between actual cost and the flexible-budget amount is the total variance, then split into price/rate and quantity/efficiency components.
Direct Materials Variances
DM Price Variance = (Actual Price − Standard Price) × Actual Quantity PURCHASED | F if AP < SP
DM Quantity Variance = (Actual Qty Used − Standard Qty Allowed) × Standard Price | F if AQ < SQ
Note: Price variance is calculated at PURCHASE (for timely reporting). Quantity variance is calculated at USE. Standard Qty Allowed = Standard qty per unit × Actual units produced.

(Actual Price − Standard Price) × Actual Quantity Purchased. Isolated at purchase, not production. Measures purchasing performance — did procurement pay more or less than budgeted per unit of material?
(Actual Qty Used − Standard Qty Allowed) × Standard Price. Measures production efficiency — did the plant waste or save material vs the standard per unit?
DM Variance Example
Standard: 2 lbs per unit at $5/lb. Actual: Produced 1,000 units. Purchased 2,100 lbs at $4.80/lb. Used 2,050 lbs.

v: Standard Qty Allowed = 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 lbs
DM Quantity Variance = (2,050 − 2,000) × $5.00 = 50 × $5 = $250 Unfavorable

4-14.title: DM Variances — Both
4-14.v:
Standard: 3 lbs of steel per unit × $4/lb = $12/unit
Actual: 12,000 units produced. Purchased 40,000 lbs @ $4.20/lb.
Used 37,500 lbs.

DM Price Variance = (4.20 − 4.00) × 40,000 = $8,000 U (unfavorable, paid more)
DM Quantity Variance = (37,500 − 36,000) × $4 = $6,000 U (used 1,500 lbs extra)
Total DM variance: $14,000 U
Direct Labor Variances
DL Rate Variance = (Actual Rate − Standard Rate) × Actual Hours | F if AR < SR
DL Efficiency Variance = (Actual Hours − Standard Hours Allowed) × Standard Rate | F if AH < SH
Standard Hours Allowed = Standard hours per unit × Actual units produced.
(Actual Rate − Standard Rate) × Actual Hours. Measures whether labor cost per hour was higher or lower than standard — driven by wage rates, skill mix, overtime.
(Actual Hours − Standard Hours Allowed) × Standard Rate. Measures productivity — did workers take more or fewer hours than standard for the output achieved?
DL Variance Example
Standard: 0.5 hours per unit at $18/hr. Actual: Produced 1,000 units. Actual hours 480 hrs at $19/hr.

v: DL Rate Variance = ($19 − $18) × 480 = $1 × 480 = $480 Unfavorable
Standard Hours Allowed = 0.5 × 1,000 = 500 hrs
DL Efficiency Variance = (480 − 500) × $18 = (−20) × $18 = $360 Favorable

4-14.title: DL Variances — Both
4-14.v:
Standard: 2 hrs per unit × $20/hr = $40/unit
Actual: 12,000 units produced. Actual hours 25,000 @ $21/hr.

DL Rate Variance = (21 − 20) × 25,000 = $25,000 U
DL Efficiency Variance = (25,000 − 24,000) × $20 = $20,000 U
Total DL variance: $45,000 U
Four Overhead Variances

r: (Actual Hrs − Std Hrs Allowed) × Std Rate
Actual Fixed OH − Budgeted Fixed OH
Budgeted Fixed OH − Applied Fixed OH

4-14.v: Actual variable OH − (Standard rate × Actual activity). Measures whether variable overhead costs per unit of the activity base were higher than expected.
(Actual activity − Standard activity allowed) × Standard rate. Same driver as DL efficiency variance — indicates the activity base itself was inefficient.
Actual fixed OH − Budgeted fixed OH. Pure spending variance — did fixed cost commitments come in above or below plan?

(Budgeted activity − Standard activity allowed) × Standard fixed rate. Reveals whether production was above or below the level assumed when computing the fixed OH application rate. NOT a controllable variance.

4-14.title: Four Overhead Variances — Worked Example
4-14.v:
Standard: 2 DLH per unit. Variable OH rate = $6/DLH. Fixed OH budgeted = $48,000 for planned production of 4,000 units (8,000 budgeted hrs → std fixed rate = $6/hr).
Actual: Produced 4,200 units (SHA = 4,200 × 2 = 8,400 hrs). Actual DLH = 8,700. Actual Variable OH = $54,000. Actual Fixed OH = $47,000.

Variable OH Spending = Actual VOH − (Std Rate × Actual Hrs) = 54,000 − (6 × 8,700) = 54,000 − 52,200 = $1,800 U
Variable OH Efficiency = (Actual Hrs − SHA) × Std Rate = (8,700 − 8,400) × 6 = $1,800 U
Fixed OH Budget = Actual Fixed OH − Budgeted Fixed OH = 47,000 − 48,000 = $1,000 F
Fixed OH Volume = Budgeted Fixed OH − Applied Fixed OH = 48,000 − (8,400 × 6) = 48,000 − 50,400 = $2,400 F (produced more than planned)

Net overhead variance: $1,800U + $1,800U − $1,000F − $2,400F = $200 U

Exam Tips: Spending & Budget variances = actual vs. what SHOULD have been spent at that activity level (control/price-type). Efficiency & Volume variances = driven by hours/activity, not price. Fixed OH Volume is the only variance NOT considered controllable — it just reflects whether actual output was above or below the level used to set the fixed rate.
Responsibility for Variances

r: Better supplier deal, rush orders, market price change
Waste, spoilage, poor quality materials, untrained workers
Using skilled workers for routine tasks, overtime premium
Machine breakdowns, poor scheduling, learning curve effects
Actual fixed costs differing from budget
Actual production above or below planned capacity

4-14.v: Journal Entries — Standard Cost System

v: Purchase DM: Dr. Raw Materials (std price) + Dr/Cr DM Price Variance | Cr. Accounts Payable (actual)
Use DM: Dr. WIP (std qty × std price) + Dr/Cr DM Qty Variance | Cr. Raw Materials
DL: Dr. WIP (std hrs × std rate) + Dr/Cr DL Rate + DL Eff Variances | Cr. Wages Payable
Apply OH: Dr. WIP (std hrs × std rate) | Cr. MOH Applied
Record actual OH: Dr. MOH Control | Cr. Various
Year-end: Dr/Cr OH variances | Cr/Dr COGS (or prorate)

4-14.v: Favorable vs Unfavorable

FAVORABLE variance = actual cost < standard cost = good news. UNFAVORABLE variance = actual cost > standard cost = bad news. BUT: a favorable price variance from buying cheap materials can CAUSE an unfavorable quantity variance if the cheap materials have more waste.

facts: Actual material used: 16,000 kg @ $5.80/kg · Actual DL: 9,500 hrs @ $21/hr
4-14.q: Calculate DM Price, DM Quantity, DL Rate, and DL Efficiency variances.
4-14.insight: Price variances belong to PURCHASING. Quantity/Efficiency variances belong to PRODUCTION. A favorable price + unfavorable quantity often signals cheap-but-defective materials.

4-14.v: Exam Tips: Price/Rate variances = calculated at the ACTUAL quantity (purchased for DM, worked for DL). Qty/Efficiency variances = compared at STANDARD price/rate. Standard Qty/Hours Allowed = standard per unit × ACTUAL units produced (not budgeted). Favorable = actual < standard. Unfavorable = actual > standard. Overhead Volume Variance = only exists under ABSORPTION costing — measures production vs planned capacity.

Actual cost < Standard cost — improves operating income. But favorable variances are NOT always good: a favorable material price variance from switching to inferior suppliers can trigger unfavorable quantity variances downstream.
Actual cost > Standard cost — reduces operating income. Investigate whether unfavorable variances stem from external factors (market prices), process issues, or unrealistic standards.

4-15.v: Why Cost Estimation?
The process of predicting future costs based on past cost behavior and expected activity levels — using methods like High-Low, Regression, or Account Analysis.

Managers need to predict future costs for budgeting, pricing, and decisions. Cost estimation methods determine the fixed and variable components of a mixed cost. The three main methods are: High-Low, Scatter Diagram, and Regression Analysis.
Comparison of Methods

r: Lowest — may be distorted by outliers

4-15.v: Estimates fixed and variable cost components using ONLY the highest and lowest activity data points. Fast but throws away all other data — vulnerable to outliers. Formula: Variable rate = (High Cost − Low Cost) / (High Activity − Low Activity).
Statistical method using ALL data points to fit a cost line: Y = a + bX. More accurate than High-Low; also produces R², t-stats, and standard errors that reveal how reliable the estimate is.

Regression is a least squares method: it fits the cost line y = a + bx by minimizing the sum of the SQUARED vertical distances between each data point and the line. This least-squares fit gives the most accurate estimate of fixed cost (a, the intercept) and variable cost per unit (b, the slope) because it uses ALL data points — unlike high-low, which uses only two.
Manual classification of each expense account as fixed, variable, or mixed based on manager judgment. Fast and cheap; accuracy depends entirely on the classifier's knowledge of the business.
Builds cost estimates from scratch using industrial engineering studies of the actual production process. Most accurate; most expensive. Used for new products where no historical cost data exists.
Regression Analysis
Regression analysis uses statistical techniques to fit the BEST LINE through all data points. It gives the most accurate cost equation by minimizing the sum of squared deviations.
Y = a + bX   |   a = Fixed Cost (intercept), b = Variable Cost Rate (slope), X = Activity Level

4-15.title: Simple Regression Output
4-15.v:
Regression of overhead cost on machine hours across 24 months yields:
  OH = $12,400 + $8.75 × MH
  R² = 0.87 · Std Error = $2,100 · t-stat on slope = 11.2

Interpretation:
  Fixed OH ≈ $12,400/month
  Variable OH ≈ $8.75 per machine hour
  R² = 87% → machine hours explain 87% of overhead variation (strong)
  t-stat > 2 → slope statistically significant
For a month planning 3,000 MH: Predicted OH = 12,400 + 8.75(3,000) = $38,650
Key Regression Statistics

r: % of cost variation EXPLAINED by the activity driver
Probability the result is due to chance

4-15.v: The proportion of variation in the dependent variable (cost) explained by the independent variable (activity). Ranges 0–1. Above 0.80 is considered strong for cost estimation; below 0.50 means the driver is a poor predictor.
Tests whether a regression coefficient is statistically different from zero. Rule of thumb: |t| > 2 → significant at ~95% confidence. Weak t-stats mean the driver may just be noise.
Multiple Regression
Simple regression uses ONE independent variable (e.g., machine hours). Multiple regression uses TWO OR MORE variables to predict cost — more accurate when costs are driven by multiple factors.
Example: Total cost = $5,000 + $3(machine hours) + $2(labor hours). Both machine hours AND labor hours drive costs.
Learning Curve Effect

As workers gain experience producing a product, labor time per unit DECREASES. Each time CUMULATIVE production DOUBLES, average labor hours per unit decrease by a fixed percentage (the learning rate).
When cumulative output doubles, AVERAGE time per unit = previous average × learning rate
When cumulative output doubles, INCREMENTAL (last) unit time = previous last unit time × learning rate

The observation that unit labor time (or cost) DECREASES by a constant percentage every time cumulative output doubles. Applies to new, labor-intensive, complex products — assembly work is the classic example.
The AVERAGE time per unit across all units produced so far declines by the learning percentage each time volume doubles. Preferred model in cost accounting exams.
Only the TIME FOR THE LAST UNIT declines by the learning percentage each doubling — average time falls more slowly than the cumulative-average model. Better fit for some real-world manufacturing.
Two Learning Curve Models Compared

KEY DIFFERENCE: Cumulative Average Model applies the learning rate to the AVERAGE of all units produced. Incremental Unit Model applies the learning rate to the LAST UNIT produced. The cumulative average model is more commonly tested on the CMA exam.

Exam Tips: Regression is MOST accurate — uses all data points. High-Low is LEAST accurate — only 2 points. R² close to 1.0 = strong relationship. R² = 0.85 means 85% of cost variation is explained by the activity. Learning curve: output doubles → average time drops by learning %. 80% learning curve is common exam example.

4-15.title: 80% Cumulative Average Learning Curve
4-15.v:
First unit takes 100 hours. Learning rate 80%.

Cumulative units | Cumulative avg time per unit | Total time
  1              | 100                          | 100
  2              | 100 × 0.80 = 80              | 160
  4              | 80  × 0.80 = 64              | 256
  8              | 64  × 0.80 = 51.2            | 409.6

The 8th unit costs 409.6 − 256 = 153.6 hrs? No — 8 total takes 409.6.
Time for units 5–8 (4 units) = 409.6 − 256 = 153.6 hrs → 38.4 hrs/unit average.

4-15.scenario: A precision-parts shop bid on a new aerospace contract for 128 custom brackets. Historical data on similar work showed an 85% learning curve. The lead estimator used a straight-line cost estimate (100 hrs × 128 = 12,800 hrs) which produced an uncompetitive bid.
4-15.question: Was the estimator ignoring the learning curve effect?
4-15.insight: Applying the 85% cumulative-average model: cumulative avg time at 128 units = 100 × 0.85^7 = 32 hrs/unit → total 128 × 32 = 4,096 hrs. That's a 68% reduction from the straight-line estimate. The bid was resubmitted at 55% of the original price and won. Actual completion came in at 4,220 hrs — within 3% of the learning-curve forecast. Now applied to all new-contract bids.

4-16.v: The coordinated management of the flow of materials, information, and finances across suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and customers to deliver value at the lowest total cost.

Supply Chain Management (SCM) coordinates the flow of materials, information, and money from RAW MATERIAL SUPPLIERS through MANUFACTURERS to END CUSTOMERS. The goal is to optimize the entire chain — not just individual companies.

r: All companies involved from raw materials to end customer
Suppliers and raw materials (before the company)
Distribution, retailers, end customers (after the company)
Small demand variations amplified upstream — causing excess inventory
Supplier monitors and replenishes customer's inventory automatically

4-16.v: The end-to-end network of suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and customers involved in bringing a product from raw material to end user. Strong SCM turns this network into a competitive advantage — fast, flexible, low-cost.

Small demand fluctuations at the customer end cause progressively larger swings upstream (retailer → distributor → manufacturer → supplier). Caused by lag, batch ordering, and forecast overreactions. Countered by real-time information sharing.

Lean management is a philosophy focused on ELIMINATING WASTE and creating value for the customer. Originating from the Toyota Production System, lean identifies seven types of waste (TIMWOOD) and works to eliminate them.

A philosophy focused on maximizing customer value while eliminating waste — anything the customer wouldn't pay for. Originated at Toyota. Guiding rule: only value-added activities remain; everything else is a target for removal.

v: T — Transportation: Moving materials unnecessarily
I — Inventory: Excess stock tying up capital
M — Motion: Unnecessary worker movement
W — Waiting: Idle time between processes
O — Overproduction: Making more than needed
O — Over-processing: More work than required
D — Defects: Errors requiring rework or scrap

4-16.v:
T — Transportation (moving material unnecessarily)
I — Inventory (holding beyond what's needed)
M — Motion (worker movement that doesn't add value)
W — Waiting (idle time)
O — Overproduction (making more than demand)
O — Over-processing (doing more than customer requires)
D — Defects (rework, scrap, returns)

v: 1. Specify Value: Define value from the CUSTOMER'S perspective — what are they willing to pay for?
2. Identify the Value Stream: Map ALL processes delivering the product — identify waste in the entire flow
3. Create Continuous Flow: Production flows SMOOTHLY without interruption or queuing
4. Establish Pull: Produce ONLY what is needed, WHEN it is needed — demand-driven (JIT)
5. Pursue Perfection: Continuously strive for zero waste, zero defects — kaizen mindset

4-16.v: SMED — Single Minute Exchange of Dies
Reduces machine SETUP/CHANGEOVER time to under 10 minutes (single-digit minutes).

v: Internal tasks: Done while machine is STOPPED — convert to external where possible
External tasks: Done while machine is RUNNING — prepare beforehand
Benefits: Faster response to demand, smaller batch sizes, less downtime, supports JIT
Lean Work Cells: U-shaped workstations. Workers cross-trained for multiple tasks. Reduces walking waste, improves communication, allows quick rebalancing

Poka-Yoke (Mistake Proofing): Devices/methods that PREVENT errors or immediately detect them. Examples: plug that only fits one way, sensors that stop machines if parts missing. Goal: eliminate possibility of human error

4-16.v: Traditional costing records costs at each stage (purchase → WIP → finished goods). Backflush costing DELAYS recording until products are COMPLETED or SOLD, then 'flushes back' to assign costs.

v: Used with JIT because inventory is near zero — no need for detailed WIP tracking
Trigger point: completion of goods OR sale of goods
Eliminates most WIP journal entries — greatly simplifies accounting
Weakness: Less detailed cost information during production

4-16.title: Backflush Costing — Journal Entries Example
4-16.v:
A JIT plant uses backflush costing with two trigger points: purchase and completion/sale. Standard cost = $50 material + $30 conversion = $80/unit. 10,000 units are purchased-for, completed, and sold this period (near-zero inventory, as expected under JIT).

1) Materials purchased: Dr Raw and In-Process (RIP) Inventory $500,000 / Cr Accounts Payable $500,000
2) Conversion costs incurred: Dr Conversion Costs Control $300,000 / Cr Wages Payable/OH $300,000
3) Backflush at completion (10,000 × $80 = $800,000): Dr Finished Goods $800,000 / Cr RIP Inventory $500,000 / Cr Conversion Costs Applied $300,000
4) Sold immediately (JIT): Dr COGS $800,000 / Cr Finished Goods $800,000

Notice: no separate WIP account, and no entry ever tracks partially-completed units — that's the simplification backflush costing trades for less real-time cost visibility.

Exam Tips: Lean 5 Principles: Value → Value Stream → Flow → Pull → Perfection. SMED = setup time under 10 minutes. Internal = machine stopped. External = machine running. Poka-yoke = PREVENTS errors. Backflush costing = used with JIT, records costs at completion/sale not each stage. JIT is PULL; Traditional MRP is PUSH.

4-17.v: Just-in-Time (JIT) System
JIT is a pull-based production system where materials and products are produced or purchased ONLY when needed — in the exact quantity needed, at the exact time needed.

A production system where materials, components, and finished goods arrive JUST as they are needed — no earlier, no later. Radically reduces inventory carrying costs but requires flawless supplier reliability and quality.

4-17.title: JIT Impact on Inventory
4-17.v:
Before JIT: 45 days of raw material inventory · Avg value $1.8M · Carrying cost @ 20% = $360k/yr
After JIT: 3 days of raw material · Avg value $120k · Carrying cost @ 20% = $24k/yr
Annual savings: $336,000 — plus freed-up warehouse space.
Trade-off: any single supplier delay stops the line. Redundant suppliers become essential.
JIT Benefits & Risks

v: Benefits: Reduced inventory costs, less waste, faster production, higher quality, lower storage costs
Risks: Supply chain disruptions can halt production (no buffer stock), requires reliable suppliers, needs stable demand

4-17.v: Kanban System
Kanban is the signal system used in JIT. Cards (kanban) authorize production or movement of materials only when needed — preventing overproduction.

Exam Tips: JIT = pull system (demand-driven). Traditional = push system (forecast-driven). JIT goal: zero inventory, zero defects. 7 wastes = TIMWOOD. Kanban = authorization card for JIT. TOC bottleneck = the WEAKEST LINK — focus all improvement efforts here. JIT requires reliable suppliers and stable demand. Main JIT risk = supply disruption.

facts: Considering JIT: reduce to 3 days of supply
4-17.q: What are the main benefits and the single biggest risk of moving to JIT?
sol: BIGGEST RISK: A supplier delay of even ONE day halts production entirely — no buffer stock exists to absorb disruption.
4-17.insight: JIT trades inventory-carrying cost for supply-chain risk. Only viable with reliable suppliers, stable demand, and short lead times. Kanban signals authorize production only when needed.

4-17.v: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)
An integrated software system that unifies ALL business functions — finance, HR, manufacturing, sales, procurement, inventory — into ONE real-time database.

ERP systems integrate ALL business functions — finance, manufacturing, HR, sales, procurement, and inventory — into ONE unified database. This eliminates data silos and provides real-time information across the organization.
Material Requirements Planning (MRP)
MRP is a PUSH-based production planning system that uses the Master Production Schedule (MPS) to determine WHAT materials to order, HOW MUCH to order, and WHEN to order them.

v: Master Production Schedule (MPS): What finished products to make and when
Bill of Materials (BOM): List of all components needed to make each product
Inventory Records: Current stock on hand and on order
MRP Output: Purchase orders and production orders

4-17.v: Net Requirements = Gross Requirements - On-hand Inventory - Scheduled Receipts

A production planning system that calculates what materials to order and when, based on the Master Production Schedule, Bill of Materials, and current inventory. First-generation manufacturing software — focus is materials only.

4-17.title: MRP Calculation
4-17.v:
Master Schedule: assemble 500 chairs in Week 8
BOM: each chair needs 4 legs
Required legs in Week 8: 500 × 4 = 2,000
Current inventory: 800 legs · Lead time from supplier: 2 weeks
Net requirement: 1,200 legs · Order timing: Week 6
MRP creates the purchase order automatically.
MRP II (Manufacturing Resource Planning)
MRP II extends MRP to include CAPACITY PLANNING, labor scheduling, machine scheduling, and financial planning. It integrates manufacturing with the broader business.

Extends MRP to include LABOR, MACHINE CAPACITY, and FINANCIAL PLANNING alongside materials. Answers "can we actually build this schedule?" — not just "what materials do we need?" Bridge to modern ERP.
ERP vs MRP vs MRP II

Enterprise-wide integrated software covering finance, HR, sales, procurement, manufacturing, inventory, CRM. One database, real-time data, single truth. Modern examples: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle Fusion, Microsoft Dynamics 365.
Benefits & Risks of ERP

v: Benefits: Real-time data, eliminates duplicate entry, better decision-making, improved inventory management, integrated financial reporting
Risks: Very expensive to implement, long implementation time (1-3 years), requires major process changes, data migration challenges, high training costs, implementation failures are common

4-17.v: Exam Tips: MRP = materials planning only (push system). MRP II = adds capacity and labor. ERP = entire enterprise integration. MRP uses BOM + MPS + inventory records. Net Requirements = Gross Requirements - On Hand - Scheduled Receipts. ERP biggest risk = implementation failure (cost overruns, disruption). JIT = pull system; MRP = push system.
Real-time visibility across all functions; standardized processes; better decision-making; reduced data errors; faster financial close; scalability across geographies.

Extremely high implementation cost (millions for large firms); 18–36 month deployments; business process disruption during rollout; user resistance; dependency on the vendor; customization can undermine future upgrades.

4-17.title: ERP Implementation Reality
4-17.v:
Mid-market ERP project (400 users):
  Software license: $600,000
  Implementation partner: $1,800,000
  Internal team time (18 months × 8 staff): $1,200,000
  Training + change management: $400,000
  Total investment: ~$4M
  Expected annual benefit: $1.2M (payback ~3.5 yrs)
  BUT 65% of ERP projects run over budget/schedule per Gartner data.

4-17.scenario: A food-processing conglomerate with 6 factories ran separate legacy systems in each plant. Consolidating monthly financial statements took 12 days; inventory information was 48 hours stale by the time HQ saw it; each factory ordered raw materials independently, losing volume discounts.
4-17.question: Was the fragmentation costing more than an ERP would cost?
4-17.insight: A 22-month SAP S/4HANA rollout cost $9.2M but delivered: monthly close cut from 12 to 4 days; centralized procurement of 8 key raw materials saved $2.1M annually in volume rebates; inventory levels dropped 18% (better forecast visibility). Payback achieved in year 3. The lesson: ERP is worth it when integration savings genuinely exceed the enormous implementation cost — verified BEFORE signing, not hoped for after.

4-17.v: Outsourcing Decisions
The strategic decision to have an EXTERNAL supplier perform an activity previously done internally — driven by cost, quality, focus on core competency, or capacity constraints.

Outsourcing means having an EXTERNAL supplier perform an activity previously done internally. It is a strategic decision that goes beyond simple cost comparison — it involves competitive advantage, risk, and long-term strategy.
Financial Analysis: Make vs Outsource
Outsource if: Outside Cost < Total Avoidable Internal Cost (variable + avoidable fixed costs)
Key: Only AVOIDABLE costs are relevant. Allocated fixed costs that continue regardless are IRRELEVANT.

The purchase price PLUS incremental in-house costs (freight in, quality inspection, coordination) MINUS opportunity cost recovery from redeploying the freed capacity to a better use. Not just "supplier quote vs current cost".

4-17.title: Outsourcing Financial Analysis
4-17.v:
Current in-house cost per unit: $45 (of which $12 is UNAVOIDABLE fixed OH)
Outsource quote: $38/unit · Freight-in $1.50 · Extra QC $0.50
Freed factory space could be leased for $80,000/year at 20,000 units of freed capacity

Relevant IN-HOUSE cost: $45 − $12 = $33/unit
Relevant OUTSOURCE cost: $38 + $1.50 + $0.50 = $40/unit
Straight comparison: KEEP in-house — cheaper by $7/unit.
Include opportunity cost: Outsourcing frees $80k/20,000 = $4 per unit equivalent → still keep in-house by $3.
Add strategic risks (dependency, quality drift, IP): case for keeping is stronger.
Qualitative Factors in Outsourcing

v: Quality control: Can supplier maintain required quality standards?
Reliability: Will deliveries be on time? Supply chain risk?
Confidentiality: Will proprietary information be protected?
Core competency: Is this activity a strategic competitive advantage? (Don't outsource core competencies!)
Flexibility: Can we quickly switch back if needed?
Workforce impact: Effect on employee morale and retention

4-17.v: Core competency at risk of erosion? Supplier reliability history? IP protection? Quality track record? Delivery lead times? Geopolitical risk (currency, tariffs, trade policy)? Cultural fit? These can outweigh a favorable financial analysis.

Exam Tips: Outsource if outside cost < avoidable internal cost. Allocated fixed costs IRRELEVANT. Don't outsource CORE COMPETENCIES. Cost leadership = minimize costs. Differentiation = invest to maintain uniqueness. Customer profitability = CM - cost to serve. BSC = 4 perspectives (Financial, Customer, Process, Learning). Strategy drives cost management decisions.

facts: Currently produces 20,000 circuit boards internally at $18/unit
Variable cost: $12 · Avoidable fixed: $3 · Allocated fixed (unavoidable): $3
External supplier quote: $16/unit for the same board
Freed capacity could rent to another division for $30,000/year
4-17.q: Should TechGear outsource? Show the analysis.
sol: AVOIDABLE cost to make = $12 + $3 = $15/unit (NOT $18 — allocated fixed continues)
Add opportunity benefit if outsourced: $30,000 rental income
4-17.insight: Only AVOIDABLE costs are relevant. Allocated fixed costs that continue whether we make or buy are IRRELEVANT. Opportunity cost of freed capacity is ALWAYS relevant.

4-18.v: Types of Capacity
The maximum output a facility can produce. Four measures: THEORETICAL (perfect), PRACTICAL (allows for normal downtime), NORMAL (long-run average demand), EXPECTED (next period's forecast).

r: Maximum output under PERFECT conditions — 24/7, no breaks, no defects
Theoretical capacity minus NORMAL downtime (breaks, maintenance, holidays)
Average expected capacity over 2-3 years considering seasonal fluctuations
Used for budgeting and POHR calculation
Capacity actually used in the current period

4-18.v: Maximum output assuming perfect conditions — no breakdowns, no maintenance, no setup, no idle time, 24/7 operations. Unattainable in reality; used only as a benchmark.
Theoretical capacity minus unavoidable interruptions (planned maintenance, holidays, normal setup time). Represents realistic maximum output. Preferred base for computing fixed cost per unit.
Average level of production expected over several years, considering seasonal and business cycle fluctuations. Smooths out year-to-year variation — good for pricing decisions.
Production forecast for the CURRENT year only. Reflects known market conditions, current backlog, workforce plans. Used for short-term budgeting.
Capacity Level and its Effect on the Financial Statements

The denominator chosen for the fixed overhead rate changes the rate, which changes how much overhead is applied, which changes reported inventory and operating income. This is the heart of D.4 — capacity choice is an ACCOUNTING decision with financial-statement consequences.

Overhead is UNDER-applied whenever actual overhead incurred exceeds overhead applied — typically when production comes in lower than anticipated. It is OVER-applied when production runs higher than anticipated.

r: Income and inventory balances VARY with the activity level used to set the rate
Prorated across WIP, FG and COGS
Income is the SAME regardless of the activity level used — proration plus the amount allocated reproduces the actual rate

4-18.v: The practical consequence: if the variance is closed out entirely to COGS, using MASTER-BUDGET or NORMAL capacity produces HIGHER operating income than using theoretical or practical capacity — and that holds whether overhead ends up over- or under-applied. Larger denominators (theoretical, practical) give a lower rate, so less overhead is capitalised into inventory and more lands in expense.

Exam Tips: Proration should be based on the overhead ALLOCATED DURING THE CURRENT PERIOD, not on the period-end balances in the accounts. And remember the headline rule: prorate → activity level does not affect income; close to COGS → it does.
Relevant Costing for Short-term Decisions
Relevant costs are FUTURE costs that DIFFER between alternatives. Irrelevant costs are the same regardless of the decision and should be IGNORED.

r: Real economic cost of choosing one alternative
Differ between alternatives — affect the decision
Can be eliminated by choosing an alternative

4-18.v: Make or Buy Decision
Should we make a component internally or buy it from an outside supplier?
Buy if: Outside Price < Avoidable Cost to Make | Consider qualitative factors (quality, reliability, strategic importance)

Compare RELEVANT costs of internal production against external purchase price. Include: avoidable fixed costs, opportunity cost of freed capacity, and QUALITATIVE factors (supplier reliability, quality control, IP protection).

4-18.title: Make-or-Buy Numbers
4-18.v:
Component X: currently made internally.
  DM $12 · DL $8 · Variable OH $5 · Allocated fixed OH $9 = $34/unit
Outside supplier offers: $28/unit

Naive answer: Buy — saves $6/unit.
CORRECT analysis:
  Only $3 of the $9 fixed OH is avoidable if we stop making it.
  Relevant internal cost = $12 + $8 + $5 + $3 = $28
  BUY price = $28 → BREAK-EVEN. Decide on qualitative factors.
  Bonus: if the freed capacity can produce a $10 CM/unit product → BUY wins.
Special Order Decision
Should we accept a one-time order below normal selling price?
Accept if: Special Order Price > Variable Cost per unit (AND there is excess capacity) | Fixed costs are irrelevant if capacity exists

A one-time order at a price BELOW normal selling price. Accept if the incremental revenue exceeds incremental cost AND accepting doesn't disrupt the regular market or use scarce capacity that would earn more elsewhere.

4-18.title: Special Order Accept/Reject
4-18.v:
Regular price: $50/unit. Regular COGS: $35 (includes $10 fixed OH).
Special order: 5,000 units at $32 each. Current capacity: 20% idle.

Wrong analysis: Reject — $32 < $35 COGS.
Right analysis: Only variable cost is relevant. Variable cost = $25.
  Incremental revenue: 5,000 × $32 = $160,000
  Incremental cost: 5,000 × $25 = $125,000
  Incremental profit: $35,000 → ACCEPT
(Assuming no cannibalization of regular sales.)
Keep or Drop a Segment
Should we eliminate an unprofitable product, division, or segment?
Drop ONLY if: Avoidable fixed costs + lost CM > 0 (i.e., dropping improves profit) | Allocated fixed costs are IRRELEVANT
Constrained Resource Decision
When production is limited by a scarce resource, maximize contribution margin PER UNIT OF CONSTRAINT (not per unit of product).
Rank products by: CM per unit of scarce resource = CM per unit / Resource units required per unit

Fixed overhead: $600,000/year
Theoretical capacity: 60,000 units → $10.00/unit
Practical capacity: 50,000 units (allows for maintenance) → $12.00/unit
Normal capacity: 40,000 units (long-run average demand) → $15.00/unit
Expected capacity: 35,000 units (next year's forecast) → $17.14/unit
Choosing a LOWER denominator (normal/expected) inflates product cost — used defensively. Choosing THEORETICAL understates cost — rarely used for reporting.

Exam Tips: Relevant costs = future + differential. Sunk costs NEVER relevant. Opportunity costs ALWAYS relevant. Special order: accept if price > variable cost AND excess capacity exists. Make or Buy: compare outside price to AVOIDABLE costs only. Keep or Drop: allocated fixed costs are IRRELEVANT. Constraint decision: rank by CM per unit of constraint, not CM per unit.

When a limited input (machine hours, skilled labor, raw material) prevents producing all profitable products, prioritize by CONTRIBUTION MARGIN PER UNIT OF THE CONSTRAINED RESOURCE — not per unit of product.

4-18.title: Constrained Resource Ranking
4-18.v:
Machine A is the bottleneck (only 1,000 hrs available)
Product X: CM $40/unit · 2 hrs on Machine A → $20 CM/hr
Product Y: CM $30/unit · 1 hr on Machine A  → $30 CM/hr

Ranking by CM per unit: X wins (higher). WRONG.
Ranking by CM per bottleneck hour: Y wins.
Fill demand for Y first, then use remaining hours for X.

4-18.scenario: A textile manufacturer operated at 62% of practical capacity. A large hotel chain approached with a special order for 40,000 sheet sets at $18/set — well below the normal $28 selling price. Sales team recommended rejecting: "we'd lose $10 per set." Regular customers were unaffected geographically.
4-18.question: Was rejecting the order the right call?
4-18.insight: Cost breakdown: Variable production $11 + Variable S&A $2 = $13/set. Fixed OH allocated at $8/set was IRRELEVANT — the capacity to make these sets already existed and cost the same whether used or idle. Incremental profit: 40,000 × ($18 − $13) = $200,000. The order was accepted after correcting the analysis. Next quarter's income statement showed a $190k boost — exactly what relevant costing had predicted. The sales team was retrained on the difference between full cost and relevant cost.

4-19.v: Michael Porter's Value Chain identifies PRIMARY and SUPPORT activities that create value for customers. Cost management focuses on optimizing each activity.

v: Primary Activities (directly create value): Inbound Logistics → Operations → Outbound Logistics → Marketing & Sales → Service
Support Activities (enable primary activities): Firm Infrastructure, HR Management, Technology Development, Procurement

4-19.v: Inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, and service — the activities that directly create and deliver the product. Each is a candidate for cost or differentiation advantage.
Firm infrastructure, HR management, technology development, and procurement — enable the primary activities. Overhead costs live here; process improvement here has cascading benefits.

r: Customer WILLINGLY pays for it — changes form, fit, or function
Customer would NOT pay for it if they knew — waste
Required by business but not valued by customer (e.g., accounting, compliance)

4-19.v: Value Chain Analysis — The Three Steps
Value chain analysis is the disciplined process of working through the chain to find where the company can create more value or spend less doing it. Hock sets it out as three sequential steps.

v: STEP 1 — Identify the activities that add value to the finished product. Which activities these are depends on the industry and on what the company actually does (manufacturing, resale, or service).
STEP 2 — Identify the cost driver (or drivers) for each activity.
STEP 3 — Develop a competitive advantage, either by increasing the value delivered to the customer or by reducing the cost of the activity.

4-19.v: A three-step examination of the firm's activities — identify value-adding activities, identify each activity's cost driver, then build competitive advantage by raising customer value or lowering activity cost. It answers WHERE in the chain the company should compete, not just what a product costs.

r: Improves established products as well as developing new ones.
Efficient assembly yields high quality at lower cost, raising operating income.
Informs customers (raising the utility they attribute to the product, supporting a higher price) and feeds customer needs back to R&D.
Controlling the flow of goods from suppliers eliminates the need to carry large inventories — lower inventory cost is value created.
Tracking inventory and sales lets the company stock the right mix and drop slow movers.
Responsive after-sale service creates superior value and can support a price premium.

4-19.v: Value chain analysis also works ACROSS companies. A complete value chain may span a parts manufacturer, an assembler, a wholesaler, and a retailer. Which part of that chain a company should occupy is decided by comparative advantage — where it can deliver the most value at the lowest cost.

Exam Tips: The three steps in order — (1) identify value-adding activities, (2) identify the cost driver for each, (3) build competitive advantage by adding value OR cutting cost. Step 2 is the one candidates forget. Note that value chain analysis can be applied INSIDE one firm or ACROSS a multi-company chain.

facts: Vertically integrated: spins yarn, weaves fabric, cuts and sews garments, and operates 12 retail stores
Spinning earns a 4% margin; weaving 6%; garment assembly 9%; retail 22%
Competitors buy yarn on the open market at prices at or below Nile's own spinning cost
Retail floor space is capacity-constrained and fully utilised
4-19.q: Apply value chain analysis. Where should Nile compete?
sol: STEP 1 — Value-adding activities: spinning, weaving, assembly, retail.
STEP 2 — Cost drivers: spinning = kg of fibre; weaving = metres woven; assembly = labour hours; retail = square metres of floor space.
STEP 3 — Spinning adds the least value (4%) and confers no advantage: competitors buy equivalent yarn at or below Nile's cost, so Nile is not the low-cost producer of that link.
Exit or outsource spinning; redeploy the freed capital into retail, the highest-value constrained link.
4-19.insight: Value chain analysis is a decision about WHICH LINKS to occupy. Owning more of the chain is not the same as creating more value — a link where you hold no comparative advantage destroys it.

4-19.v: Strategic cost management aligns COST MANAGEMENT decisions with the company's COMPETITIVE STRATEGY. There are two basic strategies:

r: Aggressive cost reduction, efficiency, economies of scale
Offer unique value customers pay premium for
Invest in quality, R&D, service — don't cut costs that support differentiation

4-19.title: Strategic Cost Management — Applied Example
4-19.v:
A furniture maker can save $2/unit ($200,000 across 100,000 units/yr) by switching to a cheaper adhesive — but it would slightly reduce joint durability, a feature customers notice.

Cost-leadership competitor: takes the switch. The $200,000 savings directly supports its strategy of being the lowest-cost producer, and a small quality tradeoff is acceptable since price is the customer's main decision driver.

Differentiation competitor: rejects the switch, and instead spends $200,000 on R&D for a stronger proprietary joint — protecting a $15/unit price premium on the same 100,000 units ($1,500,000 in premium revenue). Cutting a visible quality feature would undermine the very differentiation customers pay for.

Same cost-saving opportunity, opposite decisions — because strategic cost management means every cost decision is filtered through the company's chosen competitive strategy, not evaluated on cost savings alone.

Exam Tips: Value Chain = Primary + Support activities. Primary activities directly create value. Non-value-added activities = waste → eliminate. Bullwhip effect = demand distortion growing upstream. Benchmarking = comparing to best practices. BPR = radical redesign (vs Kaizen = gradual improvement). SCM goal = optimize the ENTIRE chain, not just one company. Customer defines what is value-added.

4-20.v: What Is Process Analysis?
The systematic examination of a business process to identify inefficiencies, waste, and improvement opportunities — using tools like flowcharts, value-stream maps, and cycle-time analysis.

Process analysis examines how work flows through an organization to identify inefficiencies, waste, and opportunities for improvement. It is a core tool in lean management and business process improvement.
Business Process Improvement Tools

v: Process Mapping / Flowcharts: Visualize the current process to identify waste and bottlenecks
Benchmarking: Comparing performance to best-in-class competitors or industry standards
Business Process Reengineering (BPR): Radical redesign of processes for dramatic improvement
Kaizen: Continuous small improvements by all employees
Six Sigma (DMAIC): Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control

4-20.v: Japanese for "continuous improvement". Small, incremental improvements made continuously by front-line workers — not big-bang re-engineering projects. Complements target costing: target costing sets the initial cost; kaizen drives cost down further during production.
📎 Full Kaizen Costing treatment — formulas, the standard-vs-kaizen comparison table, and a worked example — is in Lesson 4-21 (Quality Management).
Business Process Reengineering (BPR)

'Reengineering' originally meant taking a product apart in order to redesign it. Applied to organisations, it means restructuring processes in response to rapidly changing technology and competition. Management starts with a CLEAN SHEET OF PAPER and redesigns the process to meet the objective. Obsolete operations are discarded — not automated.
Radical, fundamental redesign of a business process starting from a clean sheet, aimed at dramatic improvement. Set out by Michael Hammer and James Champy in Reengineering the Corporation.

Hammer and Champy's argument: businesses are still run on the assembly-line model of the early 1900s. Division of labour produced huge productivity gains then, but it has left FRAGMENTED PROCESSES — one department does a piece and hands off to the next. Passing work around slows completion, adds cost without adding value, and blunts responsiveness to customers.

v: The failure mode BPR targets: using computers to AUTOMATE an outdated process rather than changing the process itself
Scope: order fulfilment, purchasing, customer service — not only manufacturing
Character: radical and discontinuous — contrast with kaizen, which is incremental
Risk: high. A clean-sheet redesign disrupts the organisation and can fail outright

4-20.v: Benchmarking Process Performance

One of the best ways to develop the distinctive competencies behind competitive advantage — superior efficiency, quality, innovation, and responsiveness — is to identify and adopt BEST PRACTICES. Benchmarking is how that is done.

Measuring the organisation against the products, practices, and services of its most efficient global competitors, or against other segments of the same company. Those standards — best practices — become the target or model for the firm's own operations.

v: STEP 1 — Identify the CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS: the aspects of performance essential to competitive advantage. These depend on the type of competition the firm faces.
STEP 2 — Set up a cross-functional team, drawn from different areas with different skills.
STEP 3 — Perform BEST PRACTICE ANALYSIS: investigate and document best practice for the processes behind those critical success factors.
STEP 4 — Identify what needs improvement and implement it, using the benchmarked company's experience.

4-20.v: The benchmarked company DOES NOT need to be in the same industry. Firms are recognised as leaders in specific capabilities — Nordstrom in retailing, Ritz-Carlton in service, Apple in innovation — and any of them can be a benchmark for that capability.

v: Benefit: establishes standards to measure against, driving continuous improvement in operations, services, and products
Benefit: identifies where improvement is needed, then measures progress in those key areas
Benefit: improvements can include cutting cost, increasing output, and improving quality
Limitation: copying a best practice from a firm with a different strategy or cost structure may not transfer

4-20.v: Exam Tips: BPR = RADICAL, clean sheet, discontinuous, high risk. Kaizen = SMALL, continuous, low risk. Benchmarking = comparison against best-in-class, and the benchmark firm need NOT be in your industry. Benchmarking starts with identifying critical success factors.
Process Mapping (Flowcharts)
Process maps visually document every step in a process — showing inputs, activities, decisions, and outputs. They reveal where waste occurs and where improvements can be made.

v: Current State Map: Documents the process AS IT IS TODAY — reveals all waste and inefficiencies
Future State Map: Shows the IDEAL process after improvements are implemented
Gap Analysis: Identifies what needs to change to move from current to future state

4-20.v: A visual diagram of every step in a business process — inputs, decisions, activities, outputs. Standard symbols (SIPOC, swim lanes) reveal handoffs, wait times, and rework loops that hide inside operational descriptions.

A specialized lean process map that also captures timing (cycle time, wait time, value-added ratio) and information flow (schedules, orders). The output is a "current-state" map and a "future-state" map showing target improvements.
Value Stream Mapping (VSM)
VSM is a lean tool that maps the ENTIRE flow of materials and information from supplier to customer. It shows both value-added and non-value-added time, identifying waste in the entire value stream.

r: Time to complete ONE unit from start to finish
Total time from customer order to delivery (includes waiting)
Actual time spent working on the product (value-added)
Available production time / Customer demand rate — the production PACE needed
Process Time / Lead Time — higher is better

4-20.v: Takt Time
Takt Time = Available Production Time / Customer Demand Rate
Example: Available time = 480 minutes/day. Customer demand = 120 units/day. Takt Time = 480/120 = 4 minutes/unit. Production must complete one unit every 4 minutes to meet demand.

The rate at which a factory must produce to meet customer demand. Takt = Available Production Time ÷ Customer Demand. When cycle time > takt time, you can't meet demand; when cycle time < takt time, you overproduce.

4-20.title: Takt Time Computation
4-20.v:
Shift = 480 minutes minus 60 minutes of breaks/meetings = 420 min available
Customer demand = 210 units per shift
Takt time = 420 / 210 = 2 minutes per unit

One workstation currently has a cycle time of 2.4 min per unit.
Consequence: bottleneck — output cannot exceed 175 units/shift (420/2.4).
Options: reduce cycle time to ≤2 min, or add a parallel workstation.
Throughput & Bottleneck Analysis

v: Throughput: Rate at which the system produces output
Bottleneck: The slowest process step — limits overall throughput
Improving any non-bottleneck step does NOT improve overall throughput
Only improving the bottleneck increases overall system output

4-20.v: The single resource in a process with the LOWEST capacity — it dictates the throughput of the entire system. In TOC, no other improvement matters until the bottleneck is elevated. Non-bottleneck idle time is FREE; bottleneck idle time is LOST profit.
Theory of Constraints (TOC) — Full Coverage

The Theory of Constraints (Eliyahu Goldratt) states that every system has at least ONE constraint (bottleneck) that limits its performance. Rather than optimising every process, managers should focus ALL improvement efforts on the CONSTRAINT.
The 5 Steps of TOC

r: Locate the bottleneck — the process limiting overall throughput
Get the most out of it
Maximise output from the constraint without major investment — eliminate downtime, prioritise the right products
All other processes must support the constraint — feed it at its pace, don't overproduce upstream
Invest to expand bottleneck capacity — add machinery, overtime, outsource the bottleneck operation
Once the bottleneck is resolved, a NEW constraint emerges — restart the 5-step process

4-20.v:
1. IDENTIFY the constraint.
2. EXPLOIT it — extract maximum output from the current bottleneck.
3. SUBORDINATE everything else to the constraint's pace.
4. ELEVATE the constraint — invest to add capacity here.
5. REPEAT — a new bottleneck will emerge; start over.

4-20.title: TOC Exploit vs Elevate
4-20.v:
Bottleneck: heat-treat oven running 20 hrs/day, down 4 hrs for cleaning.

EXPLOIT (no capex):
  Move cleaning to overlap with break shifts → +2 hrs runtime/day
  Preload next batch during unload → save 15 min/cycle
  Skip parts destined for scrap → don't waste oven time
Net: throughput up ~18% for zero investment.

ELEVATE (capex): buy a 2nd oven for $180k → doubles throughput.
ALWAYS exhaust exploit before elevate.
Throughput Costing (Super-Variable Costing)

Throughput costing (also called super-variable costing) is the costing approach aligned with TOC. It treats ONLY direct materials as truly variable. All other costs — including direct labor and ALL overhead — are treated as FIXED period costs.

r: DM + DL + Fixed OH + Variable OH

4-20.v: Throughput Contribution = Sales Revenue - Direct Materials Cost
Net Profit = Throughput Contribution - Total Operating Expenses (all other costs)
TOC Product Mix Decision — Throughput Margin per Bottleneck Hour
When the bottleneck limits capacity, produce the product with the HIGHEST throughput contribution per bottleneck hour first.
Throughput per Bottleneck Hour = Throughput Contribution / Bottleneck Hours Required per Unit

Example: Product A — Sales $100, DM $40, bottleneck hours 2 → Throughput/hour = ($100-$40)/2 = $30/hr. Product B — Sales $80, DM $20, bottleneck hours 1 → Throughput/hour = ($80-$20)/1 = $60/hr. Prioritise Product B despite lower total contribution.

Exam Tips: TOC 5 Steps: Identify → Exploit → Subordinate → Elevate → Repeat. Throughput costing = ONLY direct materials are product cost. All other costs (even DL) are PERIOD costs. Throughput Contribution = Revenue - DM only. Rank products by throughput per BOTTLENECK HOUR (not total contribution margin). TOC philosophy: the whole system is only as fast as its slowest step.

Process Analysis Tips: Takt Time = Available Time / Demand Rate — sets the production pace. Cycle Time = time per unit. Lead Time includes ALL time (including waiting). Value-Added Ratio = Process Time / Lead Time. VSM shows material AND information flows. Bottleneck limits throughput — focus improvement there first. Current state map shows waste; future state map shows the ideal.

Under TOC, the profit contribution of a product = Selling Price − Direct Materials only. Labor and overhead are treated as fixed operating expense. To choose product mix under a bottleneck, rank by throughput margin PER BOTTLENECK HOUR.

4-20.scenario: A precision-lens shop had six machining stages. Backlog was growing despite spending on all six workstations. Analysis showed Stage 3 (coating) had 40% less capacity than Stages 1–2 upstream and Stages 4–6 downstream. Stages 4–6 were idle 30% of the time waiting for coating output.
4-20.question: Where should the next capex go?
4-20.insight: Applying TOC 5 steps: (1) Identify — Stage 3 is the constraint. (2) Exploit — moved coating operator lunch break to a shift-change window, added a preload rack, skipped rejects → +22% throughput at $0 capex. (3) Subordinate — Stages 1–2 slowed to Stage 3's pace to stop WIP piling up. (4) Elevate — leased a second coating unit ($45k/year) rather than buying (test the constraint theory first). System throughput rose 40% in the next quarter. Revenue up $620k for the year. Bottleneck moved to Stage 5, which is now the next target.

4-21.v: What Are Quality Costs?
The TOTAL cost of achieving (or failing to achieve) quality — grouped into four categories: Prevention, Appraisal, Internal Failure, and External Failure.
Quality costs are costs associated with PREVENTING, DETECTING, and CORRECTING poor quality. The CMA exam extensively tests the four categories of quality costs and the trade-offs between them.
Four Categories of Quality Costs

r: Quality training, process design, supplier evaluation, quality circles
Inspection, testing, auditing, statistical quality control
Defects found BEFORE delivery to customer
Defects found AFTER delivery to customer
Warranty, returns, recalls, lost customers, legal costs

4-21.v: Money spent to PREVENT defects — training, quality planning, supplier certification, process design, preventive maintenance. Investing here reduces all three downstream categories. Ratio of prevention spending to total quality cost is a key management indicator.
Money spent to DETECT defects before shipment — inspection, testing, quality audits, calibration of measuring equipment. Necessary but adds no value from the customer's perspective.
Costs incurred when defects are found INSIDE the plant — scrap, rework, downtime, retesting. Cheaper than external failure, but still pure waste.

Costs incurred when defects reach the CUSTOMER — warranty claims, returns, product liability, lost sales, brand damage. Most expensive category; often understated because reputation costs are hard to quantify.
The Quality Cost Trade-off
Investing MORE in Prevention and Appraisal REDUCES Failure costs. The goal is to find the optimal total quality cost level.

v: Prevention + Appraisal = Costs of CONFORMANCE (doing it right)
Internal Failure + External Failure = Costs of NON-CONFORMANCE (fixing mistakes)
External failure is the MOST EXPENSIVE category — defects reach the customer
Prevention is the CHEAPEST long-term strategy

4-21.title: Quality Cost Trade-off
4-21.v:
Company A (low prevention): Prevention $50k · Appraisal $80k · Internal fail $300k · External fail $500k = $930k total
Company B (high prevention): Prevention $250k · Appraisal $120k · Internal fail $80k · External fail $60k = $510k total

Company B invested $200k more in prevention → total quality cost dropped by $420k.
Modern quality economics: 1$ spent on prevention saves ~$10 in failure costs.
Total Quality Management (TQM)

v: TQM philosophy: Build quality IN from the start — everyone is responsible
Zero defects goal: Continuous improvement toward perfection
Kaizen: Japanese philosophy of continuous small improvements
Six Sigma: Statistical approach targeting 3.4 defects per million opportunities

4-21.v: A management philosophy that makes quality the responsibility of EVERY employee at EVERY step — not just the QC department. Six principles: customer focus, total employee involvement, process-centered, integrated system, strategic approach, continuous improvement.
Quality Cost Report

Companies prepare quality cost reports showing the % of each category to total sales. A well-managed quality program has HIGH prevention/appraisal costs and LOW failure costs. Total quality costs should decrease over time as quality improves.

Exam Tips: 4 categories — Prevention, Appraisal, Internal Failure, External Failure. Prevention + Appraisal = Conformance costs. Internal + External Failure = Non-conformance costs. External failure is MOST EXPENSIVE. Prevention is CHEAPEST long-term. TQM = everyone responsible, zero defects goal. Kaizen = continuous improvement. More prevention spending → less failure spending.

4-21.title: Quality Cost Report Format
4-21.v:
Category           | Amount    | % of Sales
Prevention         | $180,000  |  1.8%
Appraisal          | $220,000  |  2.2%
Internal Failure   | $140,000  |  1.4%
External Failure   | $ 60,000  |  0.6%
TOTAL              | $600,000  |  6.0%

World-class target: total quality cost < 2.5% of sales.
Direction of travel matters more than absolute level — prevention should be rising as a share of total quality cost.
TQM Tools & Techniques

v: 1. Quality Circles: Small employee groups meeting regularly to identify and solve quality problems — empowers workers
2. Statistical Quality Control (SQC): Control charts to monitor processes. In-control = random variation within limits. Out-of-control = assignable cause exists
3. Histograms: Bar charts showing frequency distribution of quality measurements
4. Pareto Diagram (80/20 Rule): Ranks defects from most to least frequent. 80% of problems come from 20% of causes — focus on vital few
5. Cause-and-Effect Diagram (Ishikawa / Fishbone): Maps root causes of quality problems. Categories: Manpower, Methods, Machines, Materials (4 Ms)

4-21.v: Kaizen Costing

Kaizen (改善) means 'continuous improvement' in Japanese. Kaizen costing applies this philosophy directly to COST MANAGEMENT — setting cost REDUCTION targets each period and continuously working to achieve them through small, incremental improvements.

r: Continuously REDUCE costs below current actuals
Set annually based on standard specifications
Set as incremental reductions from current actual costs each period
Actual vs Target Reduction — did we improve enough?
Improvement — continuously lower the cost baseline
Continuous — monthly or quarterly improvement cycles

4-21.v: Japanese for "continuous improvement". Small, incremental improvements made continuously by front-line workers — not big-bang re-engineering projects. Complements target costing: target costing sets the initial cost; kaizen drives cost down further during production.
How Kaizen Costing Works

v: Step 1 — Set reduction target: Management sets a cost reduction percentage (e.g., reduce unit cost by 3% per quarter)
Step 2 — Identify opportunities: Teams analyse processes to find waste elimination, efficiency gains, materials savings
Step 3 — Implement improvements: Small changes are made continuously — no big capital investment required
Step 4 — Measure results: Actual costs tracked against the reduction target each period
Step 5 — Reset baseline: Achieved cost level becomes the new baseline for the NEXT period's reduction target

4-21.v: Key distinction: Kaizen costing is applied DURING the production phase (after the product is designed), making incremental improvements to existing processes. This contrasts with Target Costing which sets cost targets BEFORE and DURING design.
Kaizen Target Cost = Current Actual Cost × (1 - Reduction Rate%)

Exam Tips: Kaizen = continuous SMALL improvements during production. Standard costing = maintain standards. Kaizen costing = continuously REDUCE the cost baseline. Target costing = cost target set at DESIGN stage. Kaizen variance = actual cost reduction vs target reduction (not actual vs standard). Kaizen is linked to lean and TQM philosophy — eliminate waste incrementally. 'Kai' = change, 'Zen' = good.
Total Productive Maintenance (TPM)
TPM is a maintenance philosophy that aims for ZERO BREAKDOWNS, ZERO DEFECTS, and ZERO ACCIDENTS by making equipment maintenance EVERYONE's responsibility — not just the maintenance department.

r: Operators perform routine maintenance on their own equipment — cleaning, lubricating, inspecting
Scheduled preventive maintenance before failures occur
Cross-functional teams eliminate specific equipment losses
Key TPM metric: OEE = Availability × Performance Rate × Quality Rate

4-21.v: OEE = Availability × Performance Rate × Quality Rate | 100% OEE = perfect production (never achieved in practice)

TPM Goal: Move from REACTIVE maintenance (fix when broken) to PROACTIVE maintenance (prevent failures before they occur). Reduces waste from machine downtime, reduced speed, and defects caused by poor equipment condition.

A maintenance philosophy that transfers responsibility for basic machine care to operators, freeing specialists for complex tasks. Six big losses TPM eliminates: breakdowns, setups, small stops, reduced speed, defects, and startup losses.
Customer-Response Time
A good TQM system also lets a company manage TIME better. Being first to market, and responding quickly to shifts in demand, both require shorter development time and shorter response time.
The length of time between receipt of an order from a customer and receipt of the product BY that customer. It spans the whole journey — not just the time spent manufacturing.

r: Customer places order → order reaches manufacturing
Finished goods complete → product received by customer

4-21.v: Waiting time PLUS manufacturing time — the portion of customer-response time that sits inside the factory. Customer-response time = receipt time + manufacturing cycle time + delivery time.

Only actual manufacturing time is spent on value-adding activity. Total customer-response time is therefore reduced by attacking receipt time, waiting time, and delivery time — the three non-value-adding components.
MCE = Value-Added (Processing) Time ÷ Total Manufacturing Cycle Time.  An MCE of 1.0 would mean zero waiting — every minute in the factory adds value.

Order received Monday 09:00, reaches the plant Tuesday 09:00 (receipt time = 24 hrs). It waits in the queue 36 hrs, is manufactured in 12 hrs, and is delivered 18 hrs later.
Manufacturing cycle time = 36 + 12 = 48 hrs.
Customer-response time = 24 + 48 + 18 = 90 hrs.
MCE = 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25 — only a quarter of factory time adds value.

Exam Tips: Customer-response time = receipt + waiting + manufacturing + delivery. Manufacturing CYCLE time is only the middle two (waiting + manufacturing). Only manufacturing time is value-adding. MCE uses manufacturing cycle time as the denominator, not total customer-response time.
ISO 9000 Quality Standards

v: ISO 9000 = internationally recognized quality management standards (International Organization for Standardization)
ISO 9001 = main certification standard — specifies requirements for a QUALITY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
Certifies that PROCESSES are consistently managed — NOT that products are defect-free
Key principles: Customer focus, leadership, process approach, continual improvement
Benefits: International recognition, customer confidence, competitive advantage

facts: Rework of defective units caught internally: $30,000
4-21.q: Classify each cost into the four Quality Cost categories and calculate the total.
4-21.insight: $1 invested in PREVENTION saves ~$10 in EXTERNAL FAILURE. External failure costs (warranty, lost reputation) are the most damaging — they're only visible AFTER the customer is hurt.

4-21.v: Exam Tips: Pareto = 80% of defects from 20% of causes — focus on vital few. Ishikawa = identifies ROOT CAUSES — 4 Ms: Manpower, Methods, Machines, Materials. Control chart: points outside limits = process OUT of control. ISO 9001 = process certification (not product quality). Quality Circles = employee-driven continuous improvement.

International quality management standards from the International Organization for Standardization. ISO 9001 is the certifiable standard — requires documented processes, management commitment, continuous improvement, and customer focus. Not a product standard; a QUALITY SYSTEM standard.
